content: 1. A tuberculosis (TB) case may be assigned a unique identifier that is restricted to a specific part of the healthcare system, such as a treatment facility. 2. A clinically diagnosed TB case refers to a situation where a healthcare worker, such as a clinician or medical practitioner, has diagnosed TB and decided to initiate a full course of anti-TB treatment, even if the case does not meet the criteria for a definitive TB diagnosis. 3. Definitive TB cases are those where Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex is identified from a clinical specimen, either through culture or molecular methods. In countries with limited laboratory capacity, a pulmonary case with at least one positive sputum smear for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) is also considered definitive, provided there is a functional external quality assurance (EQA) system with blind re-checking. 4. Data completeness refers to the quality of data in a given field, assessing whether the information is comprehensive. This includes the proportion of cases with complete data on key variables. 5. Completeness of case reporting evaluates whether TB cases are fully registered and reported to national authorities through the surveillance system. 6. Adjusted TB mortality refers to the estimated number of deaths attributable to TB during a specific time period, expressed per 100,000 population per year, including deaths from all forms of TB. 7. Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is caused by strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis that are resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampicin. 8. A new TB case is defined as a patient who has never received TB treatment or has taken anti-TB drugs for less than one month. These patients may have positive or negative bacteriological results and may have disease at any anatomical site. 9. Presumptive TB refers to a patient presenting with symptoms or signs suggestive of TB (previously referred to as a TB suspect). 10. A previously treated TB case is a patient who has received at least one month of anti-TB drugs in the past. These cases may have positive or negative bacteriological results and may have disease at any anatomical site. 11. Probabilistic matching is a method used to estimate the likelihood that two TB cases are a true match. Records are compared based on specific fields, with each field assigned a weight, and potential matches are identified by calculating the sum of agreement or disagreement strengths between fields. 12. A pulmonary TB case involves the lung parenchyma. If a patient has both pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB, they should be classified as a pulmonary TB case. 13. Patient-based records are those where the individual patient, rather than the TB case, is the basic unit of recording. Cases or episodes of disease are linked to separate records for each individual using a unique personal identifier. 14. A numerical identifier is a unique code or value associated with an individual, such as an ID card number, social security number, or TB registration number. Multiple identifiers can be used depending on the setting and system. 15. Health expenditures that are out-of-pocket refer to direct payments made by households to healthcare providers, including gratuities and in-kind payments, for goods and services intended to restore or enhance health. 16. A health facility is any institution with healthcare providers formally engaged in TB program functions, such as referring presumptive or confirmed TB cases, laboratory diagnosis, TB treatment, and patient support during treatment. 17. The Health Metrics Network tool provides guidance on assessing a country’s health information system. 18. History of previous treatment is recorded at the time of registration, classifying patients based on whether they have previously received TB treatment and, if so, the known outcome. 19. Ill-defined causes refer to ICD codes for symptoms, signs, and conditions that are not clearly defined (e.g., ICD-9 780-799 and ICD-10 R00-R99), also known as garbage codes. 20. Implausible values in a database refer to unrealistic entries, such as an incorrect date of birth or a misspelled name. 21. Inconsistent or misclassified values occur when recorded facts about a case contradict each other, indicating that at least one fact is incorrect. 22. Invalid or unclear values often arise when data are recorded in free-text fields, leading to nonsensical entries (e.g., recording sex as under 15). 23. An inventory study for TB assesses the number of detected TB patients during a defined period by actively observing healthcare providers’ practices and calculating the proportion of detected cases not reported to health authorities. 24. The Lot Quality Assurance Sampling (LQAS) theory can be applied to test whether a country meets pre-specified acceptable levels of internal consistency, data accuracy, and completeness. The decision rule (d) determines the allowable number of unacceptable sampled units (e.g., BMUs) for the country to meet benchmarks. 25. The stricter the decision rule (smaller d), the smaller the required sample size (n). Conversely, a larger decision rule increases the sample size, reducing the advantage of small sample sizes in LQAS. 26. Sample size calculations for LQAS depend on the total number of BMUs in the country, the decision interval (d), and the allowable statistical error (α).
